correctness.rationale: Writing \(R(n)=\varphi(\psi(n))/n\) separates a totient loss factor from the Dedekind support product. For even \(n\ne2\), \(6\mid\psi(n)\), so the loss factor is at most \(1/3\), while five-prime support gives the exact upper bound \(1152/385<3\). For odd \(n\), \(2\mid\psi(n)\); if \(5\nmid n\), the support product is at most \(4608/2431<2\), and if \(5\mid n\), then \(6\mid\psi(n)\) and the support product is at most \(1536/715<3\). This proves strict inequality outside \(n=2\). The sharpness computation for \(39270\) is exact. The bundled finite checker independently found no contrary case through 200000.

originality.rationale: The closest primary source, Sándor (2005), proves a squarefree-kernel reduction and explicitly lists \(39270\) as a counterexample, but it does not state or imply that every support of size at most five is safe. Das (2023) proves a special sufficient family, while modern distribution work is asymptotic rather than an exact support threshold. Targeted semantic, web, database, and own-ledger searches found no equivalent or stronger five-prime-support theorem.

value.rationale: The minimum support size of a counterexample is a natural structural invariant for a classical failed inequality. Sándor's paper already identifies a six-prime counterexample but leaves open whether smaller support can fail. The theorem closes all infinitely many supports of size at most five at once, proves the bound is sharp, and isolates the unique equality case. This is a structural boundary theorem rather than a finite table extension.
